item.title: Franklin Graham calls on America to 'turn back' to God 25 years after 9/11: 'We still need His help today'
item.description: Franklin Graham urges America to rediscover the faith that filled churches after 9/11 as the nation marks 25 years since the terrorist attacks.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: Rev. Franklin Graham is calling on Americans to remember the extraordinary turn toward faith that followed the 9/11 terrorist attacks and to "turn back" to God as the nation marks 25 years since the day that changed the world forever.

"September 11 is a day I’ll never forget," Graham, president and CEO of the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association (BGEA) and Samaritan’s Purse, told Fox News Digital.

"It’s impossible to describe the tremendous amount of pain that I witnessed at ground zero in the aftermath. There were so many who were in shock and grieving," he added. "It is still hard to fathom the depths of evil that caused so much destruction."

As Americans commemorate a quarter-century since the attacks, Graham said his prayer is for America to rediscover her reliance on faith he witnessed in the aftermath.

REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: 9/11 IS JUST A HISTORY CHAPTER FOR A NEW GENERATION OF AMERICANS

"As we observe the 25th anniversary of this day when our world changed forever, my prayer is that America will recognize our need for God like we did after 9/11," Graham said. "Churches were full. People gathered to pray in public places."

Graham also recalled his father, the late evangelist Rev. Billy Graham, addressing the country from Washington National Cathedral during a national day of prayer and remembrance following the attacks.

"We’ve always needed God from the very beginning of this nation. But today we need Him especially," Billy Graham said at the time, according to Graham’s statement. "We’re involved in a new kind of warfare. And we need the help of the Spirit of God."

GEORGE BUSH WELCOMES TOP OFFICIALS TO HIS HOME STATE FOR 9/11 REMEMBRANCE ON 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF ATTACKS

"Just as America needed the help of God then, we still need His help today," Franklin Graham said.

Those themes are at the center of BGEA’s new 30-minute program, "A Day That Changed Our Lives Forever," hosted by Graham and featuring survivors reflecting on the attacks and the faith and hope they say emerged from the devastation.

Among them is Genelle Guzman-McMillan, the last person pulled alive from the World Trade Center rubble.

Guzman-McMillan spent 27 hours buried beneath the ruins, unable to move and unsure whether she would survive.

While trapped, she said she began thinking about her late mother and crying out to God for forgiveness and a second chance.

FOX NEWS MEDIA ANNOUNCES EXTENSIVE 9/11 ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE FROM GROUND ZERO, PENTAGON AND SHANKSVILLE

At one point, Guzman-McMillan said she could no longer endure it.

"God, are you listening to me? Please show me a sign," she recalled saying. Then something happened that she still cannot explain.

"And then someone grabbed me by my hand," Guzman-McMillan says in the special. "He told me his name is Paul."

She said Paul held her hand and reassured her.

SALVATION ARMY RESPONDER OPENS UP ON 9/11 CANCER BATTLE, PHONE CALL THAT CHANGED HIS LIFE

"You’re gonna be fine, help is on the way, I’m not gonna let you go," she recalled him saying.

As Guzman-McMillan began hearing rescuers’ radios, she said Paul encouraged her to keep calling out. Eventually, she heard a rescuer say, "I see her."

"I just knew I was going to go home," she said. "I am the last survivor, buried for 27 hours. I myself couldn’t believe that I survived it."

Guzman-McMillan said she believes the mysterious Paul was "an angel looking out for me."

"I wasn’t hallucinating, I wasn’t dreaming," she said. "I knew the conversation that I had."

I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES

"Something happened under that rubble," she added. "I found Jesus that day."

The special features another dramatic survival story from Sujo John, a father-to-be who worked on the 81st floor of the North Tower while his pregnant wife worked on the 71st floor of the South Tower.

After escaping, he spent hours believing his wife had died. Then his cellphone rang.

"I picked up that call thinking this is going to be the worst news of my life," he recalls.

9/11 HERO’S MEMORY PRESERVED THROUGH MASSIVE EFFORT TO ‘DO GOOD’ FOR VETS, FIRST RESPONDERS: ‘HIS LEGACY’

His wife was on the other end. She had been late for work by just minutes.

"She thought I was dead," he said. The two arranged a meeting place and ran toward each other. "We both survived."

Graham also recounts traveling to New York after the attacks and seeing people holding photographs of missing loved ones and desperately seeking information.

He began calling pastors and asking them to come help comfort and pray with grieving families.

FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE

That response ultimately led Graham to form the Billy Graham Rapid Response Team, which BGEA says has grown into an international network of thousands of crisis-trained chaplains who minister to people facing emotional and spiritual needs following tragedies and disasters.

Graham hosts "A Day That Changed Our Lives Forever," airing on Fox News Channel at 12:30 a.m. ET.

Twenty-five years later, Graham said his prayer for America remains clear.

"My prayer for our nation is that we will turn back to the God of Heaven who has brought us to this day and sustained us every step of the way."

item.title: Popular cruise line shuts down fan-favorite amenity during health scare
item.description: All public hot tubs and balcony whirlpools on Norwegian Prima remain closed as water testing continues following three Legionnaires' disease cases.
item.content:encoded:
A cruise line reportedly shut down hot tubs and heated whirlpools aboard one of its ships as a precaution following three cases of Legionnaires' disease involving former passengers.

The cases involved three travelers who sailed aboard Norwegian Prima, a 3,200-passenger vessel, in May and July 2026, the blog "Cruise Fever" reported.

The source of the exposure has not yet been determined.

CRUISE SHIPS WITH THE WORST CDC SANITATION SCORES REVEALED, SEE WHICH VESSELS FAILED INSPECTION

"We can confirm that three guests who sailed aboard one of our ships recently were diagnosed with Legionnaires’ disease following their travels," a spokesperson for Norwegian Cruise Line told Fox News Digital this week. 

"While it has not been confirmed if the exposure occurred on the ship or elsewhere, we are working closely with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to investigate these cases, as well as mitigate any further incidents, and have notified the appropriate guests and crew directly per the CDC’s guidance," the spokesperson added.

"We have elevated our sanitation procedures as part of our routine measures to ensure a safe environment on board and will continue to take any necessary measures to protect our guests and crew," the spokesperson continued.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Legionnaires' disease is a type of pneumonia caused by Legionella bacteria, which can spread when people inhale small water droplets containing the bacteria.

It can pose a greater risk to those over 50, current or former smokers, as well as people with chronic lung disease or weakened immune systems.

The cruise line said the ship's hot tubs and heated whirlpools would remain closed as a precaution while testing continues, according to the "Cruise Fever" report. 

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"As a precaution, all public hot tubs and private balcony heated whirlpools will remain closed and will reopen only after sampling has been completed and any necessary remediation measures have been carried out in accordance with CDC guidelines," the blog noted.

Online, people shared mixed reactions. 

"Stay out of the hot tub, the bacteria thrives in hot tubs! It's not transferable from person to person," one person wrote.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"I have never, nor will I ever, get in a public hot tub," said another Reddit user. "I’ve been on over 20 cruises and have never gotten in a single pool or hot tub on one. No, thank you!" 

"I booked this cruise over a year ago. So I'm pretty much going no matter what," the original poster wrote. "Can't say I feel great about it, though."

"The health and safety of our guests and crew is our top priority. As such, we operate at the very highest public health and sanitation standards," the Norwegian Cruise Line spokesperson added.

item.title: Netflix clarifies controversial 'neck injury' post on Charlie Kirk's assassination anniversary
item.description: Netflix denied mocking Charlie Kirk's assassination after its UK & Ireland account posted about almost suffering a neck injury on the anniversary of Kirk's death.
item.content:encoded:
Netflix informed Fox News Digital Thursday it did not intend to reference Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk's assassination in a recent post about almost suffering "a neck injury" on its UK & Ireland X account.

On Thursday morning, the account featured images from the Netflix series "The Gentlemen," which depicted lead character Eddie Horniman, played by Theo James, looking back at his partner and potential love interest Susie Glass, played by Kaya Scodelario, during Horniman's wedding to another woman.

"Nearly did himself a neck injury," the account posted.

A YEAR AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S MURDER, SOME COMICS ARE CALLING OUT JOKES ABOUT HIS DEATH

The post was bombarded by several conservative X users who accused Netflix of making a joke about Kirk, who was shot in the neck during a campus event at Utah Valley University exactly one year ago on Sept. 10, 2025.

"This is DISGUSTING Netflix appears to be subtly mocking Charlie Kirk’s ass*ssination on this anniversary of his death. Woke Netflix hates us. So glad I cancelled my subscription," Libs of TikTok wrote.

IN THE YEAR SINCE WE LOST CHARLIE KIRK, THE MEDIA HAS DONE ITS BEST TO ACT ITS WORST

"This is the company financially backing Bonehead Bob Bonta and his jihad against Paramount, by the way," former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt said.

The Federalist senior editor, John Daniel Davidson, commented, "One of the great advantages of our time is that, if you’re a conservative, your enemies are totally open and honest about their desire to kill you and destroy everything you love. It’s clarifying. They don’t intend to live peaceably with us. Fine. Then we won’t live peaceably."

"Seems hard to believe this is a coincidence. Absolutely disgusting," radio host Jason Rantz wrote.

However, in a comment to Fox News Digital, a Netflix spokesperson denied the post was supposed to be a reference to Kirk and called the comparison "ludicrous."

"This post directly references a plot point from our U.K. series, 'The Gentlemen,' which launched its second season on Sept. 3. Suggestions that it has any link to sensitive real world events are inaccurate and ludicrous," the spokesperson said.

As of Thursday evening, the post was still viewable on the Netflix UK & Ireland account.

Ahead of the one-year anniversary of Kirk's death, multiple universities drew criticism after reports of students planning "Kirkiversary" celebrations.

Though TPUSA reporter Savanah Hernandez admitted that she has more concern over her safety since Kirk's death, she told Fox News Digital she also feels more encouraged to keep reaching across the political aisle.

PETE DAVIDSON SPARKS BACKLASH AFTER EXPLICIT JOKE ABOUT SLAIN CHARLIE KIRK DURING NETFLIX ROAST

"Despite the uptick in violence and the increased threats that everybody at Turning Point USA has been experiencing after his assassination, I think we're more emboldened than ever to continue to stay on the ground because Charlie's entire thing was about having conversations with people to reach out to the other side," Hernandez said.

item.title: Country singer Ernest says he felt 'lost' after abruptly leaving Ella Langley's tour
item.description: Ernest revealed he's reconnecting with God and his faith after dropping out of Ella Langley's The Dandelion Tour to focus on his mental health.
item.content:encoded:
Country music star Ernest reconnected with his faith after taking a step back from the spotlight.

The "Gettin' Gone" singer, whose full name is Ernest Keith Smith, checked in with his fans on social media Tuesday, weeks after dropping out of Ella Langley's The Dandelion Tour.

Ernest, 27, admitted on Instagram he was "lost" and actively searching for answers in life but was grateful for the people who stood beside him with "love and support."

COUNTRY STAR STEPS AWAY FROM MUSIC TO FOCUS ON HIMSELF AFTER FAME TOOK A TOLL

"Bottom line is I was LOST… i recon I still am … but the search is on…. And that’s new to me," he shared on Instagram with a carousel of images.

"If anything, through this time, I am really starting to touch back in with my relationship with God… growing up in the church / Christian school, I would say I got a bit burnt out on it all."

KACEY MUSGRAVES ABRUPTLY CANCELS CONCERT DATES FROM MIDDLE OF NOWHERE TOUR

Ernest recognized that he spent "too long" relying "on my own (dumba--) way and thinking I can outsmart my better judgment [sic]."

"That’s not the case…. I don’t have many answers at all…. But I do know where it’s starting…. A dialogue with something greater than ME," he wrote.

"I can’t define it and don’t know if anyone really can… I just know that I have a beautiful life, family and friends that deserve me at my best. I deserve that for me too."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

He added, "I’m not preaching by any means…. But I just wanted to let yall know I’m taking this time to dig and discover. I love yall… and I love country music… Il [sic] be back to both soon!"

Last month, the country music singer announced he was dropping out of Langley's tour to focus on his health.

"The road has been dragging me down in a bad way," he shared on social media. "From mental to physical health. I am going away for a couple of weeks to get myself and my priorities back in order.

Advertisement

"I want to thank Ella for having me out on tour and wishing her the BEST in Auburn tonight and the rest of the tour."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

He added, "I look forward to coming back better and stronger. I owe it to myself and those affected by my actions. That starts now. Love y'all."

Langley has yet to address Ernest's absence on tour. The artists collaborated on her "Loving Life Again" hit, which he co-wrote with Devin Dawson.

item.title: Federal appeals court compares Trump migrant detention policy to Japanese American internment
item.description: The 4th Circuit rejected Trump's mass detention policy, comparing it to Japanese Americans' World War II internment, setting the stage for a Supreme Court showdown.
item.content:encoded:
A Trump administration policy to detain migrants on bond without a chance for release harkens back to the mass detention of Japanese Americans during World War II, a federal court said Thursday.

In a 2-1 decision, the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the administration's mass detention policy, a major part of President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda.

"Mass detention of marginalized individuals without due process harkens back to some of the darkest moments in our country’s history," the court wrote.

BIDEN JUDGE OVERRULED ON KEY TRUMP IMMIGRATION POLICY

Nine federal appeals courts have now separately ruled that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) new mandatory detention policy is illegal, concluding it could apply to recent arrivals at or near the border but not to migrants determined to be living elsewhere within the country.

Two other appeals courts have upheld it, meaning the U.S. Supreme Court is likely to take up the case in its upcoming term.

TRUMP SCORES SCOTUS ASYLUM WIN — BUT LIBERAL JUSTICE WARNS IT COULD BACKFIRE AT BORDER

Immigrant rights groups say basic due process is being violated when longtime residents are denied bond hearings during removal proceedings.

"The courts have resoundingly rejected the administration’s cruel policy and its blatant disrespect for the rule of law," said My Khanh Ngo, senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. "We are thrilled for our clients and their families."

Mass arrests of suspected illegal immigrants during President Donald Trump's second term have prompted widespread protests, particularly in Democratic-led cities like Chicago. In July 2025, the administration announced it would detain every migrant found anywhere in the U.S. whom ICE determines was not granted permission to enter.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said the agency was disappointed with Thursday's decision but said it recently sought a Supreme Court review of a similar decision from the 6th Circuit.

FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS

"Opinions from the Board of Immigration Appeals and two other federal courts of appeals reflect the soundness of DHS’ legal position," the spokesperson said. "This legal position was the nail in the coffin for Biden’s catch and release policies. That is why the left and their activist proxies on the judiciary are resisting it so vigorously.

"President Trump and Secretary Mullin are now enforcing the law as it was actually written to keep America safe," the spokesperson added. "As our record in the U.S. Supreme Court demonstrates, the law is on our side."

Writing for the majority, 4th Circuit Judge Nicole Berner invoked the mass internment of Japanese Americans during World War II as a warning against sweeping executive detention authority without due process.

"The stain of these detentions on our nation — and the judiciary’s abdication of its obligation to protect basic freedoms — continues to haunt us," Berner wrote.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House and ICE.

item.title: Charlie Kirk assassination allegedly mocked on campuses across country with celebrations, look-alike contests
item.description: Charlie Kirk lookalike contests and flyers mocking his death spread across campuses from Georgetown to NYU on the anniversary of his assassination.
item.content:encoded:
Celebrations and apparent Charlie Kirk "look-alike contests" are popping up on college campuses across the country on the first anniversary of the conservative activist’s assassination with anonymous posts and flyers advertising events tied to Georgetown University, the University of South Carolina, the University of Maine and New York University, among others.

The latest apparent event surfaced in NYU’s Yik Yak community, where an anonymous user posted an image of a flyer advertising a "KIRKAVERSARY C. KIRK LOOKALIKE CONTEST" at "WSQ Park" at 10 p.m. Sept. 10, offering a $5 prize and instructing attendees to "BYOB."

The NYU post followed similar apparent contests advertised through anonymous campus social media platforms at Georgetown in Washington, D.C., and the University of South Carolina, turning what initially appeared to be an isolated controversy into a broader phenomenon surrounding the anniversary of Kirk’s killing.

DEMOCRATIC STUDENT GROUP TO PROTEST CHARLIE KIRK MEMORIAL AT CAMPUS WHERE HE WAS KILLED

Kirk, the 31-year-old founder of Turning Point USA, was assassinated Sept. 10, 2025, while speaking at Utah Valley University during his American Comeback Tour.

Students at Georgetown University allegedly planned a Kirk "lookalike contest" for the anniversary of the conservative activist’s assassination, and the event drew thousands of upvotes on Fizz, an anonymous social media platform popular with Georgetown students, according to screenshots shared with Fox News Digital from the school’s Turning Point USA chapter.

Similarly, an apparent Kirk look-alike contest called "Kirkiversary" is being advertised at the University of South Carolina for Thursday.

The screenshot featured an anonymous Yik Yak post circulating on social media advertising a "Charlie Kirk look-alike contest" on Greene Street outside USC’s Russell House at 7 p.m., offering a $50 prize and telling prospective participants, "Be there or be square."

The University of South Carolina replied to the Libs of TikTok post saying, "We have no record of any registered student organization planning such an event. No university resources will be used to support this. DM us if you’d like a contact here that can help verify claims like this ahead of posting."

Georgetown also told Fox News Digital it was not tied to the event, saying, "We have seen no activity on campus related to these posts. Georgetown is not planning such an event and, to our knowledge, no student organization is hosting or planning such an event."

REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR

Other schools appear to be celebrating Kirk’s death with images circulating on social media and shared by Libs of TikTok that appear to show flyers mocking Charlie Kirk’s death posted at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln.

The flyers include an image of Kirk and the words "REST IN PISS FOREVER MISS" and "THE MASTERBAITER." A social media post circulating the images also claims that additional flyers have been posted around campus and that events celebrating Kirk’s death are being planned.

The University of Tennessee-Knoxville also condemned messages that celebrate political violence after mysterious "Kirkaversery" [sic] flyers advertised a gathering apparently marking one year since Charlie Kirk’s assassination, declaring, "WE WILL CELEBRATE THE FIRST NEW YEAR AK (AFTER KIRK)."

At Rochester Institute of Technology, flyers circulating online by Libs of TikTok appeared to advertise a "CHARLIE KIRK LOOKALIKE COMPETITION" at the Kate Gleason dorm quad on Sept. 10 at 1 p.m., with a prize listed as "$10 + FAME + TROPHY." The flyer did specify that the look-alike contest was not affiliated with RIT.  

A second flyer advertises a "Twerk for Kirk" competition with a $10 entry fee and monetary prizes.

ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION

Libs of TikTok also shared screenshots of a series of posts appearing in the University of Maine’s Yik Yak community on the first anniversary of Charlie Kirk’s assassination.

Screenshots circulating online showed multiple anonymous posts using the term "Kirkiversary" and apparently mocking Kirk’s death and the manner in which he was killed. Among the posts visible in the screenshots are messages stating, "HAPPY KIRKIVERSARY!!!! TODAY IS A GREAT DAY!!!," "Carotid arteries out for Charlie Kirk!" and "Woke up with a horrible pain in my neck," accompanied by an image of a man experiencing neck pain.

Similarly, purported internal messages attributed to members of the UNC Charlotte university community discussing the anniversary of Charlie Kirk’s assassination were also shared on X by Libs of TikTok.

The messages, published on social media, appear to include individuals discussing how to celebrate the anniversary, joking about Kirk’s assassination and, in one instance, expressing hope that President Donald Trump would die.

REPUBLICAN CONVENTION ATTENDEES SHARE HEARTFELT TRIBUTES TO LATE CHARLIE KIRK ON ASSASSINATION ANNIVERSARY

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Wiley Norvell, senior vice president for university relations and public affairs at NYU, said, "No recognized student group is organizing any such event, nor is one taking place in an NYU building or space. University resources would never be used in this way. We are reporting these posts for misusing NYU's name. We strongly condemn any elevation of political violence."

The University of Maine told Fox News Digital in a statement that the university "condemns violence, threats of violence and rhetoric that celebrates or makes light of violence in any form. The safety of our students, employees and visitors is a top priority. We take credible threats seriously, investigate them promptly and work with law enforcement and public safety partners when appropriate.

"The UMaine chapter of Turning Point USA held an event on campus Wednesday evening. The event was approved in advance and held in accordance with established university policies and procedures governing campus events. UMaine Police were present to support campus safety and security. The event concluded without incident, and the university received no threats of violence associated with the event, either before, during or after it.

"Yik Yak is an independent, third-party open and anonymous social media platform that is not affiliated with, sponsored by, endorsed by or administered by the University of Maine. The university does not operate or control the platform and does not have access to information identifying individuals behind anonymous posts. Any credible threat involving members of the university community or campus safety is taken seriously and addressed in accordance with university policies and established public safety procedures."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

A UNC Charlotte spokesperson gave the following statement to Fox News Digital: "UNC Charlotte did not generate these messages. They were posted on Yik Yak, an anonymous third-party platform, and the university does not know who authored them. UNC Charlotte does not condone the posts. If the university receives credible information indicating that a member of our community has made a threat or violated university policy, we will review it and respond appropriately."

A University of Nebraska-Lincoln spokesperson also addressed the controversy in comments to Fox News Digital.

"The University of Nebraska–Lincoln is aware of flyers that were taped to bus stops on campus that contained imagery of the late Charlie Kirk. There is no indication that anyone affiliated with the university is responsible for the creation and/or distribution of the flyers," the spokesperson said. 

"The university does not condone or support messages making light of violence or the loss of life. The safety and well-being of our students, faculty, staff and visitors are our highest priority. The university encourages anyone who becomes aware of an immediate safety concern to report it through UNL Report or by calling University Police."

Fox News Digital reached out to Rochester Institute of Technology and Turning Point USA for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Ex-NFLer Emmanuel Acho sells out Big Dom for podcast views, putting Eagles security chief under investigation
item.description: Emmanuel Acho's podcast revelation about a car accident cover-up has triggered an NFL investigation into Eagles security chief Big Dom DiSandro.
item.content:encoded:
You never rat out the guy who fixes your messes. That is locker room rule No. 1. But podcast queen and former NFL linebacker Emmanuel Acho apparently missed the memo, trading loyalty for views.

Now Philadelphia Eagles Chief Security Officer Dom DiSandro, known as "Big Dom," faces an NFL investigation after Acho publicly recounted the incident.

On his "Speakeasy" podcast, Acho (formerly an Eagle) recounted a car wreck from his playing days in Philadelphia. He rear-ended a vehicle on his way to practice, panicked and called team security.

Instead of taking responsibility, Acho said the team allegedly manipulated the official record, effectively shining a light on Big Dom.

DIANNA RUSSINI PULLED PATHETIC MOVE WITH AN OFFICER TO GET OUT OF A TICKET, AND IT SHOULD HAVE THE NFL NERVOUS

"I hit one of our security people. He says, ‘Acho, when the cop shows up, send the cop away. I’m going to send you another cop and that other cop is going to say it wasn’t your fault, it was their fault.’ I was like, ‘Wait, they do that?’ So, I hit him," Acho said.

"Cop comes up. ‘Hey, everything good?’ I’m like, ‘Everything’s good, don’t worry about it. Somebody is going to come here.’ That cop leaves. We send another cop. The other cop that comes to document says she’s at fault. I was like, ‘Yo, this is crazy.’"

When the driver realized she had been hit by an NFL player, team security stepped in to contain the fallout.

"Our head of security had to offer them two home tickets plus signed jerseys," Acho said. "And they were like, ‘Oh, no, we’re fine.’"

According to Acho, Big Dom helped bury the incident, only for that favor to come back and put him under the NFL’s microscope years later.

DiSandro now faces heavy league scrutiny. The NFL is reportedly examining whether his alleged involvement in the incident violated league rules or exposed the Eagles to liability.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The NFL previously fined him $100,000 and suspended him from the sidelines following a 2023 dustup with 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw.

Acho sold out Big Dom’s loyalty for cheap podcast clout.

Former Eagles cornerback Asante Samuel blasted Acho online, labeling him an attention-seeking gossip queen. When a guy saves your career, you keep your mouth shut.

Samuel posted on X while reacting to the Big Dom investigation.

"Like I said before, watch who you do business with. We have an investigation going on because fool is dying for attention and a gossip queen smfh."

HOW THE DIANNA RUSSINI-MIKE VRABEL SCANDAL COULD DERAIL THE PATRIOTS' SEASON ON THE FIELD

Acho has made a habit of trading basic judgment for cheap attention. Following Charlie Kirk’s assassination, he sparked fierce backlash by publicly explaining why he refused to view the political activist as a hero.

"Charlie Kirk, he proudly stated that death by guns is a price we have to pay for our Second Amendment rights," Acho said in a reaction video.

"It almost feels like me mourning his death by gun is the opposite of what he stood for."

He added in a follow-up clip, "We have other people trying to memorialize him, and I do not believe he was a hero."

Whether preaching morality or betraying the man who covered his tracks, Acho always picks clout over code.

item.title: Undercover video exposes Dem Senate nominee's plan to embrace socialists: 'Got to be together'
item.description: Roy Cooper's North Carolina Senate race heats up as the former governor rejects calls to repudiate Democratic Socialists of America's influence.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Roy Cooper, the former North Carolina governor and a Democratic candidate for the Senate, believes his party should incorporate a big-tent approach to an emerging wave of socialist candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

When asked if he would sign the Promise to America, a repudiation of socialist stances put out by moderate Democrats, Cooper said he wouldn’t.

"I don’t see any need to," Cooper said in video footage obtained by Fox News Digital.

"I think the party needs a wide spectrum, particularly at a time when the Republican Party is shrinking and having all kinds of loyalty tests. I think we need to have all kinds of folks to be a part of our party."

FLORIDA BOARD VOTES TO BAN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS FROM PUBLIC COLLEGE ADMISSIONS

Cooper’s comment comes as he wages a bid to fill the seat of retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and win over a historically Republican-leaning state. It also raises questions of whether moderate Democrats believe their platforms can coexist with the aims of the DSA.

The DSA espouses positions like abolishing the U.S. Senate, establishing public ownership of corporations and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), according to its website.

The group paints a picture of what those policies could look like in practice on its website.

"You have no debt. You don’t need health insurance. You don’t pay a mortgage or have a landlord, because comfortable housing is a human right. Your retirement is publicly funded. Food, education, energy, medicine and transportation aren’t for-profit businesses; they are common goods and utilities," the group states.

Cooper is not affiliated with or backed by the DSA and has pitched himself as a candidate with an ability to reach across the aisle. His campaign has highlighted his ability to work with a Republican-controlled legislature during his tenure as governor from 2017 to 2025.

In his own words, Cooper has pushed back on questions about being tied to the DSA.

TRUMP HERALDED AS GOP 'KINGMAKER' AFTER LOUISIANA SENATE RESULTS RATTLE PARTY ESTABLISHMENT

"For the record, no," he told The New York Times about whether he was a communist. "I have a record of working across the aisle. The people of North Carolina know that I can be a senator that puts them first. Before power, before party, before politics. I feel confident that, at the end of the day, they’ll send me to Washington."

When asked if Cooper’s platform is at odds with the DSA’s views, Cooper’s campaign declined to comment, noting that his commitments are reserved for his constituents.

"The only pledge Roy makes is to the people of North Carolina. Roy is not a socialist, and he will work with anyone, including Republicans, as he has done his entire career to lower costs for hardworking families and fight for North Carolina," his campaign told Fox News Digital.

Some Republicans are skeptical of that reasoning.

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, believes moderates are afraid to challenge their progressive flank as candidates championing the far left have surged in the 2026 midterm primaries.

"That dynamic is dangerous right now because they are terrified of the extreme left. Finding a middle ground on ideological issues right now is … the prospects for success, particularly between now and election day, are not high," Cruz said at an energy summit hosted by Club for Growth and Arnold Ventures Thursday.

"Schumer is truly terrified right now," he added, referring to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.

In the video interview, Cooper said he believes the party will only weaken itself in its resistance to the administration if it doesn’t band together.

TRAFFIC DRAMA THREATENS TO END DEM GOVERNOR'S TENURE AS VOTERS HEAD TO POLLS IN RHODE ISLAND

"Particularly now when we’re in such difficult straits, and we’re in a foxhole right now. We’ve all got to be together to take our government back," Cooper said.

"We could fall to the autocracy anytime we don’t stick together. So, I don’t see the need signing something."

Having secured the Democratic nomination, Cooper now heads to the Nov. 3 general election, where he faces Republican nominee Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee.

item.title: Falcons quarterback problems deepen as Tua Tagovailoa suffers oblique strain at practice
item.description: Tua Tagovailoa's oblique strain at practice thrust Cooper Rush into first-team reps as the Atlanta Falcons face a potential Week 1 quarterback crisis.
item.content:encoded:
The quarterback conundrum continues for the Atlanta Falcons this week following Tua Tagovailoa’s injury at practice.

The Falcons are considering Tagovailoa, who was named the starter in Week 1 by default it seemed with Michael Penix Jr. still not ready to play, day-to-day after suffering an oblique strain.

Tagovailoa was limited at practice, while Cooper Rush, his backup heading into Week 1, received first-team reps in new head coach Kevin Stefanski’s offense.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

This adds a whole new wrinkle to the Falcons’ quarterback situation, which was heavily discussed throughout the preseason, and not in a good way on Tagovailoa’s part.

It was reported that Atlanta’s wish was for Penix to ease his way back into his starting role as the team’s franchise quarterback, while Tagovailoa, whom the Falcons acquired after he was released by the Miami Dolphins, held down the fort until then.

But Tagovailoa’s inconsistent practice and preseason play worried the Falcons about whether that plan was sufficient to begin the regular season. It got to the point where it was believed the Falcons’ job was Penix’s to lose, granted he was healthy enough to go.

Penix is coming off a torn left ACL he suffered in Week 11 of last season, ending his year prematurely. It was also the third ACL tear of his career, dating back to his days in college.

If Tagovailoa is unable to go on Sunday, Rush, who has started 16 games across his eight seasons in the league, will very likely be thrust in there to start the season. Jack Strand, who signed with the Falcons as an undrafted free agent this offseason, could back him up.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Tagovailoa was spotted grabbing at his back during the media viewing portion of practice after throwing a pass in a drill. His movement was reportedly quick and he sat down on the grass before ultimately jogging off. He didn’t attempt a pass for the remainder of the media portion, as Rush took his spot in drills.

"I’m not sure what happened, but it’s Thursday practice," Rush said, via ESPN. "Practice has to go on and so you’re up next and that was a good day. It was good to get out there and get some real reps with that group and we’ll see what happens."

Rush noted that this was his first significant workload with the Falcons’ first-team offense since signing with the team.

"The mindset of the prep really never changes," he added. "The only thing that changes is that I think you get more prepared because you get to practice, you get reps, you get walk-through reps. I think it helps a lot."

We’ll see how Tagovailoa’s injury progresses by the weekend, but Stefanski’s Falcons debut might come with a quarterback who would ordinarily be third string if everyone were healthy.

item.title: Bioweapon threat exposed as Anthropic sounds alarm on foreign actors plotting virus experiments
item.description: Researchers outside the United States used Anthropic's Claude to plan gain-of-function experiments on bird flu, chikungunya and dangerous toxins.
item.content:encoded:
Researchers outside the United States used frontier AI models to plan experiments involving highly pathogenic bird flu, chikungunya and other biological agents with potential weapons applications, according to a new threat report from Anthropic.

The researchers used AI to study viruses’ transmissibility and immune evasion, investigate orthopoxvirus immune-response genes and help design novel toxins at times while taking steps to evade safeguards meant to restrict access to dangerous biological capabilities.

Anthropic detailed five cases in the report published Thursday but withheld the countries, institutions and specific biological agents involved. The company stressed that it is not claiming the researchers intended to develop biological weapons.

AI KILL SWITCH BILL COULD SHUT DOWN ROGUE MODELS

The findings offer a concrete glimpse at a threat that has largely been discussed in hypothetical terms. Scientists who already possess biological expertise, materials and laboratory access are using increasingly powerful AI systems to accelerate sensitive dual-use research.

They also land amid a renewed debate over catastrophic AI risks. Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher, recently resigned while accusing the companies of "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." His warning drew more than 100 million views on X.

SEN BERNIE SANDERS: YES, WE MUST HIT THE PAUSE BUTTON ON AI BEFORE IT IS TOO LATE

Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s alignment science lead, separately said he personally believed there was a greater than 10% chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade.

But Anthropic’s report points to a threat that is already taking shape: researchers using frontier AI for potentially dangerous biological work, circumventing geographic restrictions and adapting when the models’ safeguards get in their way.

In one case, Anthropic blocked a grant application for chikungunya gain-of-function research at a military research institute. The proposed work focused on identifying mutations that could increase the virus’s transmissibility and ability to evade the immune system.

The researchers planned to engineer those mutations into infectious clones and repeatedly pass the virus through live animals, selecting for variants that caused the most severe disease.

That work could help scientists develop better vaccines and treatments for chikungunya. It could also produce a more dangerous pathogen that would be difficult to distinguish from a naturally occurring outbreak, Anthropic said.

The researchers accessed Claude through a life sciences platform that tunneled traffic through U.S. infrastructure to evade Anthropic’s regional restrictions. When Claude refused to answer sensitive prompts, the platform routed those requests to another model with more permissive safeguards.

Anthropic said the research continued after the company banned accounts connected to the activity. The platform operator reestablished access within days using new identities, while Claude continued to provide editorial assistance on research materials.

In another case, a researcher spent weeks using Claude to plan experiments involving mammalian adaptation and airborne transmission in highly pathogenic avian influenza.

FDA APPROVES FIRST-EVER MRNA FLU VACCINE FOR MILLIONS OF OLDER AMERICANS

The researcher was studying viral traits that could allow bird flu to spread more effectively among mammals and cause severe disease outside the respiratory system. A version capable of efficient human-to-human transmission would pose a significant pandemic threat, according to the report.

Anthropic said the researcher appeared to have access to virus isolates and animal-model facilities. The company confined the work to weaker models, limiting the assistance primarily to study design, data analysis and editorial support.

The company said the case provided evidence of an active research program developing the knowledge and biological materials needed to create pathogens with enhanced pandemic potential. The researcher also took steps to hide his identity while accessing the models from an unsupported region.

A separate user connected to a state-associated infectious-disease laboratory used Claude to draft an orthopoxvirus research grant from start to finish in about an hour.

Orthopoxviruses include variola, the virus that causes smallpox, as well as mpox. The grant application proposed studying viral genes that disable the human immune response and included the central hypothesis, experimental design, dosing, statistical plans and contingency strategies.

Because the work was framed around weakening the virus, Claude’s safeguards did not block the assistance. But Anthropic said the same knowledge could also help a researcher preserve or enhance the virus’ immune-evasion capabilities.

The final two cases involved venom peptides and toxins.

One researcher used Claude to build an atlas of toxin peptides from multiple venomous animal lineages and then created a generative pipeline to optimize their characteristics.

The stated goal was to develop new painkillers, antidepressants and other treatments. But the atlas also included structures associated with paralytic toxins that could potentially be used as incapacitating agents. Anthropic said the work was part of a state-supported research program.

In the other case, a researcher used Claude to computationally redesign several toxins, including a bacterial toxin and a protein from a hemorrhagic fever virus identified by the World Health Organization as a priority disease threat.

The researcher used Claude to help prepare progress reports but instructed the model to keep the identities of the toxins deliberately vague.

The cases illustrate why biological misuse can be difficult to prevent through automated filters alone. Anthropic’s safeguards blocked the clearest attempts involving enhanced pandemic pathogens, but they were less effective when users framed their work as medical, defensive or therapeutic research.

"Biological capabilities are dual use," Anthropic said in the report. "The same information that can be used to develop a biological weapon could also be used to develop, for example, a vaccine or a cure for a disease."

The company said it recently reviewed 30 days of activity associated with adversarial state institutions and found roughly 35 distinct biological research efforts. Most involved ordinary civilian science, but some had "notable dual-use potential."

Anthropic said the findings do not show that Claude has enabled an imminent biological attack.

They do show, the company said, that researchers tied to state-associated programs are attempting to evade access controls and use frontier AI models in biological research that could have weapons applications.

The company said future safeguards will likely require more than content filters, including identity verification, institutional vetting and closer monitoring of users seeking access to advanced biological capabilities.

item.title: Texas A&M's Mike Elko describes fight between LSU, SEC over former NFL players as 'parenting'
item.description: Mike Elko compared the SEC's clash with Lane Kiffin and the LSU Tigers to parenting, saying the school backed down once "dad raised his voice."
item.content:encoded:
The SEC, no stranger to attention, is once again the center of the college football world. Though not necessarily due to a dominant dynasty racking up championship after championship.

Lane Kiffin, also no stranger to attention, immediately invited controversy after taking over as head coach of the LSU Tigers by working to bring in former college players who have signed contracts to play in the NFL. The SEC and Big Ten immediately moved to ban pro players from playing, leading to a series of court battles to settle the issue.

While LSU ultimately prevailed, with a judge granting an injunction to let two players, Dae’quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, play this season, the SEC and other teams signaled their intention to fight back. Hard.

LSU LEAVES FORMER PRO-ATHLETES OFF FINAL ROSTER, ONE NIGHT BEFORE SEC TAKES LANE KIFFIN AND TIGERS TO COURT

The conference cited Kiffin’s flippant, sarcastic comment before halftime during the game against Clemson in a new amended complaint: "Imagine if we had pro players."

It was then widely reported that the conference’s other 15 schools would vote to kick the Tigers out at a meeting scheduled for Sept. 10.

A brief war of words ensued, resulting in the Tigers seemingly backing down by adding two non-pro players to the roster and filling out their final two spots.

Some commentators, like Stephen A. Smith, have defended LSU’s actions, while many opposing coaches have expressed a mixture of skepticism, bewilderment or anger over how Kiffin and the Tigers’ administration handled the situation.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

One of Kiffin’s rival SEC coaches, Texas A&M’s Mike Elko, just added to it Thursday with a colorful explanation of the dynamic between the two opposing sides.

"This is a little bit like the son figuring out where the limits are until dad comes home and raises his voice, and then the son goes, ‘I was just kidding, I didn’t mean any of that,'" Elko said. "I think that’s what you’re seeing. LSU will be in the SEC…This is just a little bit of parenting going on right now."

Mike Elko, never one to shy away from a great quote.

There’s some truth to that, and it’s evidenced not just by how the administration and Kiffin have handled this situation, but how the governor of Louisiana handled it too. After seemingly backing the Tigers, Gov. Jeff Landry issued a statement to Yahoo Sports! regarding the potential vote which said simply, "Ridiculous. Can we just play football?"

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Well, that’s part of the problem, isn’t it? Kiffin’s search for any advantage, no matter how minute, led the Tigers to push the boundaries of what other teams and, ultimately, fans find acceptable. For weeks, LSU backers proudly insisted they were right about bringing NFL players back to college football. As soon as the stakes were raised — for example, with the possibility of expulsion from the conference — the message became, "Can we just play football?"

The turn of phrase Elko used might be colorful, but it’s right. LSU was the upstart teenager, who got his bluff called by dad. Dad won out, and now the tone of the conversation has changed.

LSU and Texas A&M play on Sept. 26 in Baton Rouge, without any NFL players on the field. There will be, however, a must-see postgame handshake between these two coaches.

item.title: Prosecutor Joseph diGenova resigns from DOJ role investigating Trump-Russia probes
item.description: Joseph diGenova resigned from his Justice Department role investigating the alleged "Grand Conspiracy" surrounding the Trump-Russia investigations.
item.content:encoded:
Joseph diGenova has resigned from his Justice Department role investigating the alleged "Grand Conspiracy" surrounding the Trump-Russia investigations, according to two sources familiar with the matter. 

Fox News has learned diGenova had lost the confidence of both the Justice Department and the White House. According to sources familiar with the matter, he had been effectively sidelined well before his departure.

His resignation comes after months in which his role had diminished internally, ending his involvement in the investigation amid questions about his standing within both the administration and DOJ leadership.

ABC News first reported his resignation. 

"It was an honor and a privilege to serve the president and the department," diGenova told CBS News. 

He declined to comment further on the circumstances surrounding his departure.

DiGenova’s wife, attorney Victoria Toensing, who also joined the federal prosecution team in South Florida, is expected to leave the Justice Department on Friday, according to CBS News.

DOJ ORDERED TO FREEZE ANTITRUST WORK WITH CANADA AS TRADE TENSIONS INTENSIFY

The so-called "Grand Conspiracy" investigation is based out of the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Fort Pierce, Florida. It examines whether Obama- and Biden-era officials were involved in a long-running effort to prevent Trump from returning to political office.

The probe has scrutinized officials involved in past investigations of Trump, including former CIA Director John Brennan and former FBI Director James Comey. DiGenova was also overseeing a separate criminal investigation into whether Brennan lied to Congress about the intelligence community’s assessment that Russia interfered in the 2016 election.

MAJOR BLUE STATE HOSPITAL PULLS PLUG ON CONTROVERSIAL CHILD TRANSGENDER TREATMENTS AFTER DOJ INTERVENTION

The investigation has issued dozens of subpoenas over the past year. Lawyers for some witnesses were recently notified that their clients would receive grand jury subpoenas, while investigators also sought voluntary interviews with former FBI agents involved in the Mar-a-Lago investigation, according to CBS News. Prosecutors have not filed charges in either case.

DiGenova was tapped to oversee the probe in April after career prosecutor Maria Medetis Long was removed from the case. He had criticized delays in the investigation and said indictments could have been brought within 30 days.

His departure, along with Toensing’s expected exit, leaves the future of the investigation uncertain.

The longtime Washington attorney previously served as U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia from 1983 to 1988. He later represented Trump’s campaign during its unsuccessful effort to challenge the 2020 election results.

This is a developing story. Check back later for updates.

item.title: Dolly Parton’s sister reveals ‘last thing’ country legend asked of her before death
item.description: Stella Parton said that prayer was the last thing her sister, Dolly Parton, asked for before her death from a brief battle with cancer.
item.content:encoded:
Dolly Parton's sister is sharing the final request she received from the musician.

During a recent interview with "CBS Mornings," Stella Parton shared the last thing her sister asked of her before her death.

"That’s the last thing Dolly asked me for, was prayer," she recalled.

The legendary musician died Aug. 25 at the age of 80 after a "brief battle with cancer," which she hid from her fans and even some family members.

DOLLY PARTON OFFERED TO TRY EXPERIMENTAL DRUGS IF ‘NO HOPE’ FOR CANCER BATTLE TO HELP OTHERS, SISTER SAYS

Stella noted that the family would not be sharing what type of cancer Dolly had "out of respect for her" since Dolly "didn't tell us that we could say it." She added that she is able to speak about her love for her sister, but when it comes to her health, "it's not my business to tell her business."

Concerns over the "Jolene" singer's health first arose in September 2025, when she made the difficult decision to postpone a number of shows in Las Vegas, telling fans she needed to undergo a "few procedures."

"I want the fans and public to hear directly from me that, unfortunately, I will need to postpone my upcoming Las Vegas concerts," Parton shared online at the time. "As many of you know, I have been dealing with some health challenges, and my doctors tell me that I must have a few procedures."

Shortly after Dolly made her announcement, concern among fans increased when her sister Freida asked fans to pray for Dolly, saying, "Many of you know she hasn’t been feeling her best lately."

When speaking with "CBS Mornings," Stella noted, "I think Dolly got on to Freida about that.

DOLLY PARTON’S ONGOING HEALTH BATTLE FORCES COUNTRY LEGEND TO MISS MAJOR DOLLYWOOD EVENT

"I'm pretty sure Dolly said, 'You're going to, you know, pipe it down,' because that was the first time people thought 'Oh,'" she said. "And she knew that Freida was just upset and hurt, but she thought, 'Don't be telling my situation, Freida. Don't be spilling my business.'"

According to Stella, Dolly decided to keep her diagnosis a secret because she "could not bear negative things" and didn't want her fans to worry about her.

Her death came a little over a year after the death of her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean, who died in March 2025 at the age of 82. While some have speculated Dolly died of a broken heart, Stella doesn't agree.

"I think she was very sad, but I don't think that's why she got sick," Stella said. "I think she worked too hard and didn't maybe take as good a care of herself as she should have. She, at one point, she said, 'You know, I spent a lot of time caring for Carl that maybe I neglected myself.'"

DOLLY PARTON LAID TO REST AS NIECE SHARES EMOTIONAL TRIBUTE TO ‘GRANNY’

She went on to say that while it "broke her heart to see him in the shape he" was in before he died, she ultimately believes Dolly's determination to continue working "so hard for so long" contributed to her death.

When speaking about Dolly's relationship with Dean, she referred to it as "very unique and very deep and loyal" and gave Dean credit for being supportive of Dolly and loving "her enough to let her be what she was."

Stella explained that while Dolly was a huge star across the globe, Dean "didn't care about that at all," and if it was up to him, she would have been "at the house with her hair up in a ponytail and barefooted cooking in the kitchen." Stella said even family members rarely saw Dolly without her signature glamorous look after she became a star.

"Not after she got to be Dolly Parton. No. She would sleep in her makeup when she'd come spend the night with me," Stella said. "Oh, I knew what she looked like. She looked like me without her makeup. So, I knew what she looked like without it."

Her sister also credited Dolly for being a good businesswoman, saying that while she had opinions on politics and other controversial topics, she never shared them because "she would never have offended anyone."

Although Dolly was battling cancer, Stella says she knows her sister was at peace in her final moments.

"She knew where she was going," she said. "She wasn't going anywhere bad. She was going to be with mom and daddy. She was prepared. Yeah, she was definitely prepared."

item.title: Nike shareholders reject transparency proposal as faith-based firm questions DEI commitments
item.description: Tim Schwarzenberger explains why Nike's perfect Human Rights Campaign score and DEI ties sparked a shareholder proposal at its annual meeting.
item.content:encoded:
Tim Schwarzenberger’s last pair of Nike sneakers is about 10 years old and the shoes have holes in them.

But the Christian investor who helped lead a shareholder campaign demanding more transparency from Nike says he wants a reason to buy another pair.

"For me, what resonates is forgiveness," Schwarzenberger told OutKick. "If companies make changes, we need to applaud them."

NIKE FORGOT THAT REPUBLICANS BUY SNEAKERS, TOO, AND NOW IT'S GETTING BOOTED FROM THE S&P 100

"I would like to get back to buying the shoes, but I can’t rationalize doing that when Nike has become so activist," he said. "If the company can change, I would be the first to applaud them and get in line."

Schwarzenberger is a portfolio manager and director of corporate engagement at Inspire Investing, a faith-based firm that represents investors who own Nike stock. Those investors make money if Nike succeeds, not if it collapses.

"We’re long-term investors," he said. "Our primary goal is to earn competitive performance for the investors we serve, and we want companies to do well."

Nike shareholders rejected Proposal 5 during the company’s annual meeting Sept. 8. Inspire backed the proposal on behalf of client William C. Cunningham.

The resolution asked Nike to evaluate and issue a report analyzing the "benefits, costs, and legal, reputational, competitive, and other relevant risks" associated with its charitable support.

The proposal’s supporting statement specifically cited Nike’s verified score of 100 on the Human Rights Campaign’s Corporate Equality Index. Inspire argued that the score raises questions about whether Nike’s employee health plan covers gender-transition procedures for minors, including surgery, cross-sex hormone therapy, menstruation suppression and puberty blockers.

Schwarzenberger said Nike has not publicly answered whether it provides those benefits to minor dependents.

HRC's 2026 criteria require transgender-inclusive health benefits for full credit, but Nike's public HRC profile does not disclose the company's age limits or dependent-specific plan terms.

The proposal also pointed to Nike’s broader DEI initiatives and argued that its charitable relationships with advocacy organizations could create legal, reputational and financial risks.

Nike’s board recommended that shareholders reject the proposal, arguing in its 2026 proxy statement that the company already evaluates those risks.

"The company’s current approach to charitable giving, together with our existing disclosures and guidelines, appropriately serves the best interests of our shareholders," Nike stated.

The company also said creating another report would consume time and resources without providing additional value to investors.

Detailed vote totals were not yet available when OutKick interviewed Schwarzenberger. Nike disclosed the results in a September 10 SEC filing, showing the proposal received less than 1% of votes cast for or against it.

"Most shareholder proposals do not receive majority support, so that was not a surprise," Schwarzenberger said. "But we were able to make the case to shareholders and raise issues that I think are on the minds of many shareholders."

Nike said charitable partnerships are approved only after what it described as a "robust due diligence review."

"Any time I hear the word robust, it kind of scares me," Schwarzenberger said. "Are they actually concerned about the end investor?"

Proposal 5 focused heavily on Nike’s relationship with the Human Rights Campaign and its Corporate Equality Index, which evaluates companies on their LGBTQ workplace policies and practices.

Nike received a verified score of 100 on the 2026 Corporate Equality Index. The Human Rights Campaign recognizes companies receiving that score as leaders in LGBTQ workplace inclusion.

Schwarzenberger said the score means Nike is complying with what Inspire considers an increasingly left-wing set of corporate requirements.

"They’re doing all the things that the Human Rights Campaign has asked for," he said. "It’s really been like a moving treadmill where they’ve upped the ante every single version. The goalposts are always switching."

Participation in the survey declined sharply this year. According to HRC’s own report, the number of Fortune 500 companies submitting information fell 65%, from 377 companies in 2025 to 131 in 2026.

HRC said the decrease in public reporting does not necessarily mean the companies changed their underlying workplace policies.

Nike remained a participant.

Schwarzenberger argued that Nike’s continued participation in HRC’s Corporate Equality Index raises questions about whether the company has adequately considered the legal, reputational and financial risks of its partnerships.

"Our ask is simply to provide transparency into what Nike is doing," he said. "If the company has analyzed the risk of these organizations, then let us see it."

"Nike is set to be removed from the S&P 100 before trading begins Sept. 21, after nearly 18 years in the blue-chip index.

S&P Dow Jones Indices said the rebalance is intended to make its indexes more representative of their market-cap ranges.

The company’s market cap has fallen by more than $200 billion since its November 2021 peak. Nike has also lost ground to newer competitors and faced product challenges, while Greater China revenue fell 13% on a currency-neutral basis in fiscal 2026.

TED CRUZ TAKES VICTORY LAP AS ICONIC AMERICAN BRAND'S STOCK PLUNGES TO 12-YEAR LOW

Schwarzenberger acknowledged that Nike’s political decisions cannot be blamed for all of that.

"It is hard to dissect exactly what is causing the share-price decline," he said. "There are many factors, including China and perhaps some missteps with the company’s approach there and with various campaigns."

Still, he believes Nike has made its recovery more difficult by taking positions that anger some potential customers.

"At the very least, don’t do things that are going to upset your customers further," Schwarzenberger said. "If you are alienating half of your customer base, it is difficult to quantify exactly what percentage of the share-price decline is caused by those activities. But it is certainly a distraction."

OutKick has previously detailed Nike’s history with Colin Kaepernick, the canceled Betsy Ross sneaker, Dylan Mulvaney and a proposed study involving transgender youth athletes.

Schwarzenberger said Nike does not need to move toward conservative politics to correct course.

It just needs to stop making politics part of the product at all.

"The company does not need to take sides," he said. "It does not need to go right or left. It needs to stay in the middle, focus on its business and acknowledge its mistakes."

Schwarzenberger said Nike CEO Elliott Hill’s comments about refocusing on athletes were encouraging, but not strong enough to convince him that the company was committed to changing course.

"The CEO’s statement at the annual shareholders meeting about focusing on the athlete was good, but it was kind of a lukewarm response," he said. "They really need to take a very strong approach and say, ‘Look, we’re going to focus on manufacturing athletic apparel, and that’s going to be our focus. We’re not going to wade into hot-button political issues.’"

He also wants Nike to produce better products.

"If Nike does that and begins showing innovation in its products, that would be progress," he said. "Nike should get back to focusing on its core business and show that it is not an advocacy organization. It is an apparel company."

Schwarzenberger compared Nike’s lack of product innovation to Disney’s reliance on brands from the 1990s.

"It’s kind of like Disney. When’s the last time you’ve seen a good Disney movie?" he said. "We’d like to see some innovation."

Schwarzenberger said Inspire filed dozens of shareholder resolutions last year, and roughly two-thirds of the targeted companies made the changes the firm requested.

That leverage is not limited to professional investors. Millions of Americans own shares in major companies indirectly through mutual funds held in their 401(k) accounts. Fund managers generally determine how those shares are voted in corporate elections.

item.title: Fatwas, holy wars and socialism: Inside the Islamic conference where El-Sayed drew a hero’s welcome
item.description: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed headlined an ISNA conference where an attendee called for a fatwa against members of Congress.
item.content:encoded:
DETROIT, Mich. — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed headlined an Islamic conference over Labor Day weekend where the United States was described as an empire in decline, early Islamic conquests were praised and the aftermath of 9/11 was framed around Islamophobia and discrimination.

The event, held annually by the Islamic Society of North America, featured a range of speakers discussing topics from Muslim civic participation to the ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas. 

Over the course of the conference’s speeches and panel discussions, participants took positions that were generally critical of the United States and the broader Western world and expressed opinions that some may regard as extreme.

EXILED MUSLIM SCHOLAR WARNS FAR-LEFT–ISLAMIST ALLIANCE BEHIND ANTI-ISRAEL PROTESTS ECHOES IRAN’S RISE

Fox News Digital attended the event over the weekend, sitting in on many of the panels held on Saturday and Sunday before and after El-Sayed's speech. The Michigan Democrat is running in one of the most hotly contested Senate races of the 2026 cycle, the outcome of which may decide control of the Senate.

At one panel, "Rising Islamophobia in the U.S.," a speaker described recently passed legislation that could bar colleges participating in certain commercial boycotts of Israel from receiving some federal higher education funds as "an anti-Muslim bill."

Shortly after that, a man in the audience wearing a Pakistani flag pin stood up and called for a fatwa to be issued against the bipartisan group of lawmakers who voted for the bill. A fatwa is a religious ruling or opinion that can range from a formal condemnation to, in some cases, a call for or justification of violence.

The legislation was introduced by Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., and co-sponsored by Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.

After the man called for a fatwa against members of Congress, members of the audience — and one panelist — applauded.

Earlier, during the same discussion, a panelist criticized Congress for moving to censure Reps. Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib for making "​​the most lighthearted comments"

Tlaib was censured in part for endorsing the phrase "from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free," which calls for the destruction of Israel as bounded by the Jordan River in the east and the Mediterranean Sea in the west. Critics characterized the phrase as a call for ethnic cleansing, while the congresswoman defended it as "an aspirational call for freedom, human rights and peaceful coexistence."

ISNA is a nonprofit Muslim religious organization established in 1981 to provide America's growing Muslim population with a platform for civic coordination and education. Detroit, where the event took place, is situated in a metropolitan area that has a significant Arab American population concentrated in areas such as Dearborn and Hamtramck.

EL-SAYED CAMPAIGN BACKED BY OVER $100,000 FROM DOZENS OF MEMBERS OF GROUP WITH ALLEGED TERROR TIES

Panelists also accused billionaire Elon Musk of funding a White supremacist global anti-Muslim movement, suggested that some of the narrative regarding 9/11 taught in American schools has been "debunked" and asserted that Muslims were treated unfairly in the wake of the 2001 attacks.

Criticism of America’s response to 9/11 surfaced repeatedly across the conference’s events and breakout sessions. One speaker asserted that one of the most important things to reflect on as the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approaches is that "Islamophobia is at an all-time high." Another called the War on Terror, a series of post-9/11 military operations that claimed the lives of over 7,000 U.S. military personnel, the "War of Terror."

El-Sayed has sought to moderate his public image since launching his Senate campaign, even as he has maintained ties to prominent socialists and socialist-aligned activists. His attendance at the recent ISNA conference is the latest in a series of associations that have drawn criticism, including ties to Nation of Islam figures, Muslim clerics accused of expressing support for terrorist organizations and activists on the socialist left.

In response to these charges, the Democrat has pointed out that GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers has links to individuals who echo conspiracy theories about the 2020 election or who have called for bans on gay marriage.

EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS

Before the event, El-Sayed’s campaign moved to distance the candidate from other conference speakers.

"Abdul is not affiliated with and does not endorse any other participant of the conference," a spokeswoman for his campaign told media outlets in the lead-up to the event.

The statement followed reports that he would appear alongside Islamic clerics who defended child marriage and praised U.S.-designated terrorist organizations, including al Qaeda. Of the controversial speakers, only the cleric who had defended child marriage was ultimately disinvited, The Washington Free Beacon previously reported.

ISNA appeared to anticipate scrutiny over some of the speakers it invited to the conference. In the conference venue’s main hallway, the organization posted a prominent sign which says, "ISNA does not endorse the actions of convention participants and explicitly disclaims any responsibility for the views expressed, information provided, or materials displayed, sold or distributed by convention speakers, performers, exhibitors, vendors, or attendees."

COUNTERTERRORISM EXPERT WARNS ABDUL EL-SAYED SENATE BID RAISES HOMELAND SECURITY CONCERNS

While ISNA sought to distance itself from the controversial views expressed by some conference speakers, the organization itself took actions that also drew scrutiny.

Fox News Digital spoke to three Christian evangelists outside the conference who claimed they were removed from it without warning. Each of them said they were simply having conversations with individuals who wanted to speak with them before they were escorted outside by security.

Attendance at the conference was open to people of all faiths, and registration did not require attendees to be Muslim. The conference also held an interfaith banquet on Sunday.

The disclaimer took on added significance in light of books available for purchase at the conference’s on-site bazaar. Fox News Digital found books that defended Islamic warfare while portraying Christianity as uniquely violent.

"Christians are the last people on earth who should bring the charge of bloodshed and cruelty against followers of any other system, for it is a well-established fact that no religion known to history has such a horrible sanguinary record as church Christianity," one book sold at the conference reads.

Another book argued that all Islamic warfare is defensive, defended non-Muslims being forced to pay a discriminatory tax and claimed that Christian civilization has killed nearly 200 million people by attributing wars that did not have religious motivations or were not initiated by Christians. 

The French Revolution, which was instigated by individuals hostile to Christianity, for instance, is counted toward Christianity’s death count. The Korean War, which was launched by communist North Korea, is also counted toward the body count of Christianity.

UNEARTHED INTERVIEW REVEALS EL-SAYED’S SHARIA ‘OBLIGATION’: ‘NOT BECAUSE OF FEAR’

The conference also featured advertisements for "Sharia-compliant" mortgages and other financial products.

El-Sayed held a quasi-celebrity status among the conference’s attendees. Campaign buttons were nearly ubiquitous at the conference, and his campaign’s booth was easily the busiest of those located in the main hall, Fox News Digital found.

When the Senate hopeful walked on stage to address the conference, he was greeted with a thunderous standing ovation. Calls of "we love you" rang out from the crowd.

El-Sayed’s speech was ultimately measured and largely focused on unity, representation and the idea that Muslim and American identities are compatible.

"As we leave here tonight, I’ve got a challenge for each and every one of you," El-Sayed said with a measured cadence reminiscent of former President Barack Obama. 

"It’s the question of how you show up in the spaces in which you show up everyday, as wholly and 100% yourself. Because we are a community as Muslim Americans who believe in the rhyming of our Muslim ideals and our American ideals. That those two things are not mutually exclusive, in fact, that at their best being Muslim makes us better Americans and being Muslim enables us to be better Americans."

‘DESTROYING THE AMERICAN WAY OF LIFE’: EL-SAYED’S POLITICAL ORBIT COMPLICATES EFFORT TO MODERATE HIS IMAGE

But elsewhere at the conference, speakers offered a markedly different assessment of America and its place in the world.

"The world has become multipolar, and we see almost like the fear and insecurity that the empire has at this moment if we think through the lens of the U.S. So, I like to think that we are on the very end of an ending empire," an academic speaking at a session about the conflict between Israel and Hamas said. "I'm very positive about it."

The same panelist later argued that referring to the river next to Detroit as the "Detroit River" was an immoral act of colonialism because Native Americans had a different name for the waterway.

In a similar vein, a speaker at one of the conference’s main sessions criticized American foreign policy after the 9/11 terrorist attacks, then credited the "TikTok generation" with mobilizing in favor of Palestinians following the Oct. 7 terrorist attacks.

Some speakers, however, made a clear effort to connect El-Sayed’s socialist project with his Islamic faith.

"Islam historically was not just spread by the instance of Dawah. It was spread by socialism," said a cleric who would go on to speak positively about early Islamic conquests.

ISNA declined comment. The El-Sayed campaign did not respond to requests for comment after being reached by Fox News Digital Wednesday.
