item.title: Suzy Kolber opens up about ESPN firing, emotional reaction: 'I lost it'
item.description: Suzy Kolber revealed the emotional phone call and non-disparagement clause that followed her ESPN layoff after 27 years hosting "Monday Night Countdown."
item.content:encoded:
Suzy Kolber was part of a 20-talent layoff at ESPN in June 2023, along with Steve Young, Max Kellerman and Jalen Rose. At the time, Kolber hosted the network’s "Monday Night Countdown" pregame show.

Kolber spoke about her firing for the first time during a conversation on the "Sports Media with Richard Deitsch" podcast this week.

"He [ESPN president Jimmy Pitaro] said, ‘Suzy there’s a whiteboard and your name’s on it. I don’t really know for sure right now but your name is on it,'" she said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

It’s unclear how the head of the company didn’t know whether Kolber was safe. Nonetheless, she recalled coming home that night and having a conversation with her daughter.

"I remember that day sitting next to my daughter in the kitchen. For years I’ve said ‘You never know.’ And I sat down next to her and I cried. And I said, ‘I think this is really happening.’"

The following week, Kolber received a call from then-ESPN executive Norby Williamson, best known as a supporter of Mark Jones.

Kolber said she "lost it" when Williamson told her she couldn’t say "anything disparaging about the company or we can take the last year of your contract."

Before her layoff, Kolber had agreed to take a pay cut.

"I did think the 39% cut was going to get me to the end [of my career]," she said.

Perhaps Kolber should have remained silent about her firing. She didn’t help herself with these comments.

For one, she comes off as entitled. We understand that a layoff can be emotional, regardless of the circumstances. However, a non-disparagement provision is standard. Kolber is no different from any other talent laid off with time remaining on their contract.

There was hardly a reason to "lose it," as she put it, over the clause.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Kolber also worked at ESPN for 27 years. She is now 62. She hosted the network’s top pregame show. ESPN didn’t owe her anything else. And yet, she suggested that she was unhappy with the lack of appreciation she received during her departure.

"I just thought after 27 years of, I was the first person hired for the launch of ESPN 2. I was the first person assigned to the X Games," she continued. "I went and shot the marketing tape for it. ‘Monday Night Football’s’ move to ESPN, I was part of some pretty big franchises. You’re not going to say a word? Not thanks for 27 years, just acknowledge it? I didn’t understand that."

At least her bosses didn’t fire her on-air, mid-show, as they did Ryan Clark in an apparent attempt to spite OutKick.

Our understanding is that Kolber’s firing was about the numbers. The network needed to shed a certain amount of talent salary, and she became expendable because ESPN employed other anchors who could fill her role. ESPN eventually tapped Scott Van Pelt to replace Kolber on "Countdown."

ESPN likely would have made a change at the position regardless, with its first-ever Super Bowl broadcast coming this fall. The anchor of "Monday Night Countdown" will also host the Super Bowl and its halftime show.

As one of the faces of the network, Van Pelt was a favorite for the position before 2023.

The network arguably has more NFL hosts than it has major sports. Van Pelt hosts Mondays. Mike Greenberg hosts the Sunday morning pregame show. Laura Rutledge, the host of "NFL Live," would be the lead football anchor at most networks and arguably should be at ESPN.

Therefore, Kolber became the odd person out.

Still, Kolber was a good host. Her talent and production were not the issues. In fact, since executive Burke Magnus is in the business of rehiring previous anchors, he should have brought her back.

Instead — in what appears to be a make-good for firing Ryan Clark — Magnus rehired Stan Verrett, who has a weird obsession with OutKick and race talk, to anchor a show on NFL Network.

Kolber has since shifted her focus, creating a new interview series called "The Originals" on the Scripps Sports Network. Her first episode airs Sept. 15 at 8 p.m.

item.title: Comedian declares Jerry Seinfeld 'uncancellable' despite 'woke' anti-Israel festival boycott
item.description: Several performers pulled out of Lisbon's inaugural MEO Commedia a La Carte Fest after headliner Jerry Seinfeld's addition, citing support for the Palestinians.
item.content:encoded:
Several performers have pulled out of an international festival in Portugal headlined by comedian Jerry Seinfeld, with some citing concerns related to the Israel-Gaza conflict and others giving no public explanation.

The withdrawals come ahead of the inaugural MEO Commedia a La Carte Fest in Lisbon, scheduled for Oct. 29 to Nov. 1. While some acts left the lineup without a public explanation, others cited political differences with performers involved in the festival.

On Saturday, actress Inês Aires Pereira announced on Instagram that she was withdrawing her show Namastê from the festival lineup. 

In one image, Pereira wrote in Portuguese that "one of the names persistently defends ideas and acts that I consider indefensible. We cannot minimize or normalize a genocide," according to a translation by The Hollywood Reporter.

COMEDIAN DECLARES HUGH LAURIE 'CAN'T BE CANCELED' AS ACTOR COMES TO SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM'S DEFENSE

Musical comedy duo Cebola Mol also addressed their exit on Instagram, writing in a translated caption, "We will celebrate justice, freedom and joy with you on another occasion." The post included a cartoon watermelon, which is widely used as a symbol of Palestinian solidarity.

Several departing acts did not disclose their motives. High-profile performers, including pop musical project Tributo Pop, comedian Pedro Tochas, the group Conjunto Cuca Monga and visual artist Vhils all withdrew from the festival lineup without publicly stating a reason.

MICHAEL RAPAPORT SLAMS 'CLOWN' MACKLEMORE FOR ANTI-ISRAEL PERFORMANCE

Seinfeld is the festival’s main headliner and has publicly supported Israel. The festival’s website still lists him as a performer. 

His support for Israel during the conflict has drawn accolades but also fierce criticism. In June, while leaving a New York Knicks game at Madison Square Garden, Seinfeld told a streamer asking for a "Free Palestine" shoutout that "it doesn’t exist."

During an event at Duke University, Seinfeld also discussed pro-Palestinian protests, saying, "Free Palestine is, to me, just — you’re free to say you don’t like Jews. Just say you don’t like Jews.

RABID ANTI-ISRAEL ACTIVISTS SET TO HIT THE STREETS TONIGHT IN MAMDANI'S MANHATTAN

"By saying ‘Free Palestine,’ you’re not admitting what you really think," he continued. "So, it’s actually — compared to the Ku Klux Klan, I’m actually thinking the Klan is actually a little better here because they can come right out and say, ‘We don’t like Blacks, we don’t like Jews.’ OK, that’s honest."

Fox News Digital reached out to Seinfeld’s team but did not hear back.

Comedian and media analyst Tim Young argued that the withdrawals hurt the departing performers far more than Seinfeld, whom he called "uncancellable."

"It was a total eye-roll for me," said Young, who also serves as a Media Fellow at the Heritage Foundation and media editor at The Dallas Express.

"I think anybody who is a comedian, anybody who is a performer, would want to work with basically the most successful, if not one of the most successful comedians in world history at this point. The guy's a billionaire from his comedy and his writing, and I don't know why you would want to walk away from it," he added.

Young suggested the withdrawals were simply catering to their existing fan base, calling the move "a group of woke people performing for woke people."

"They know who their audience is. They're behaving the way that their audience would behave and just playing into it," he said, adding the performers are likely getting more publicity from pulling out than they would have from performing.

Young doesn't believe the withdrawals will have any lasting impact on Seinfeld's standing in the comedy world.

BILL MAHER SAYS IT’S 'SO STUPID' FOR ANTI-TRUMP ARTISTS TO BAIL ON KENNEDY CENTER PERFORMANCES

"You can’t cancel somebody like him," Young said. "Comedy is uncancellable. You get to a certain level, you're not going to be affected by it, and it’s important that people like Seinfeld … come out and say, ‘Hey, you know, this is bad, the things that are happening.'

"Adults can't be adults anymore. Everybody has to whine and cry. They will sacrifice their own success for a stupid stance."

item.content:encoded:
Alanis Morissette became one of music’s biggest stars with "Jagged Little Pill," but behind the blockbuster success was a frightening wave of hostility that she says included websites plotting her murder.

Morissette, who skyrocketed to fame after the release of her 1995 album, opened up on the "Call Her Daddy" podcast about the hostility she faced at the time, including death threats and attacks from some fellow musicians.

"There was terror and resistance, but that's just normal," the singer recalled of the response she received from her lead single "You Oughta Know."

SHANIA TWAIN CONFRONTS LONGSTANDING NARRATIVE THAT HER MUSIC PROMOTES MAN-HATING

"But you know, at that point, project onto me all you want," Morissette said. "Project that I'm the Antichrist. Project that I'm terrifying or ... basically too much. My whole life I've just heard that I'm too much."

But the backlash Morissette described went far beyond criticism of her music or personality. As her fame intensified, she recalled the hostility escalating to a chilling level.

"There was a lot of hate," she told host Alex Cooper. "There were websites constructed to figure out how to murder me most elegantly."

"Well, there was a lot of hate, and it was very, very out there. And a lot of people, a lot of artists whom I respected and lived for, were disparagingly speaking about me. Later, Sinéad apologized, which was really classy. But, yeah, I mean, it was not a girl squad. There were no girl squads."

Morissette said the hostility was particularly painful when it came from fellow artists, including musicians she admired. Among her vocal critics at the time was Courtney Love.

"I think Courtney Love was calling me fake, which is so funny," she recalled. "And she also apologized later and said very kind things."

Decades later, Morissette said she views the reaction through a different lens. She compared the resentment she encountered to modern-day jealousy surrounding Taylor Swift and argued that women were often made to feel there was room for only one at the top.

"They were upset. I was, you know, it's like people being jealous of Taylor Swift," she explained. "And I think the implication there for me was that the presupposition on the planet was that there's one throne. 'Only Alex can sit in the throne, everybody. Everyone else, you fail. You lose. You're ugly. Bye.' What? That's patriarchy. That's scarcity mindset."

Morissette started performing at a young age, including an early stint on the Canadian children’s television series "You Can’t Do That on Television." She initially found success as a dance-pop singer in Canada, but her career changed dramatically with the 1995 release of "Jagged Little Pill."

The album shot to No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and turned Morissette into an international star.

item.title: 'Morning Joe' hosts do a mock prayer for Tim Scott after 'really weird' speech at midterm convention

item.content:encoded:
A panel on MS NOW’s "Morning Joe" mockingly prayed Thursday for Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., after he gave a fiery speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.

The Republican Party is holding its first-ever midterm convention in Dallas to rally voters as the GOP fights to keep control of Congress in November.

During the convention, Scott gave a fiery speech, declaring, "The only way to keep dangerous, radical, weird out of the Senate is a united Republican Party, standing with our President, Donald J. Trump! Stand for the president, Donald J. Trump! 

CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? GOP BETS ON TRUMP AT HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION

"This is a battle for the heart of our nation. I said, the heart of our nation! The Democrats’ extreme candidates won’t rip that heart out of our chests!"

He added, "They hate our culture. They hate what it means to be American. Hear me, Dallas. Not! On! Our! Watch! We will not back down. We will not grow weary."

"Wow. You know, speaking of weird. That was really weird," "Morning Joe" co-host Joe Scarborough said. "I thought for a moment there, he needs some anti-seizure medication. I was concerned, and the whole ‘ripping the heart out of the chest’ and ‘Democrats hate America and American culture.’

AL SHARPTON RAGES AT FLORIDA GOV DESANTIS' IMPRESSION OF HAKEEM JEFFRIES

"Thank you, baby Jesus, all right," Scarborough said.

"I’m actually praying," co-host Mika Brzezinski replied.

"I am actually praying, too," Sharpton replied, saying he was shocked at Scott’s rhetoric, adding that it went far beyond merely kissing the ring.

"I understand that you bowed to Trump, but the way he really went off the chain, you’ve got to really wonder about where he is in his head. And this is — ‘overcompensation’ is too light a term — this is, I’ve never seen anything like that in national politics," Sharpton added. 

"And to play to Trump like that, you’d only do that if you were in fear of facing, you know, a firing squad or something."

Sharpton went on to blast Scott for demonizing Democrats, saying he does not do so to Republicans or even Trump.

Scarborough agreed, saying while he laments that Republicans have changed in that they are no longer in favor of "melting pot" ideals of welcoming immigrants, he does not argue that they hate America.

Nathan Brand, a spokesperson for Scott, told Fox News Digital, "Bless their hearts," in response to the "Morning Joe" segment.

item.title: Trump administration accuses prestigious law school of favoring Black applicants over White, Asian peers
item.description: Federal officials allege a major California law school favored Black applicants over Asian and White students, but the university denies violating admissions laws.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration on Wednesday blasted the University of California, Berkeley, School of Law for allegedly favoring Black applicants while discriminating against Asian and White students, marking its latest federal action targeting race-conscious admissions policies at universities.

The Department of Justice (DOJ), along with the Department of Education, found Berkeley Law in violation of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits racial discrimination in programs and activities receiving federal funds.

"The data produced by Berkeley Law demonstrates a strong bias against Asian and White applicants, with a corresponding bias in favor of Black applicants," the DOJ said.

The findings came after officials launched a compliance review of Berkeley Law in March 2025, roughly two years after the Supreme Court struck a major blow to affirmative action programs many universities used in admissions for decades. California had already banned affirmative action in public education under Proposition 209, enacted in 1996.

JUSTICE DEPARTMENT ZEROES IN ON UCLA FOR ALLEGED ILLEGAL DEI ADMISSIONS AS ELITE SCHOOL CRACKDOWN EXPANDS

According to the DOJ's analysis, Black applicants in 2025 had "5.8 times higher odds of admission than comparable white applicants."

An analysis of LSAT scores for admitted students in 2024 and 2025 found that 37% of Black admitted applicants scored below 99% of admitted White applicants.

In addition, half of the school's admitted Black applicants had LSAT scores "below 95% of the admitted white applicants."

According to figures cited by the DOJ, median LSAT scores from 2021 through 2025 showed a persistent disparity between racial groups, with Black admits scoring around 165. Asian and White admits scored around 172, while Hispanic admits had median scores around 169.

"The median Black admit consistently has an LSAT score about 5 points lower than the median white or Asian admits," the department said in a letter to attorney Tania Faransso, who is representing the law school.

DOJ OPENS PROBE INTO PRESTIGIOUS COLLEGE OVER ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION FAVORING MINORITY STUDENTS

As of October 2025, Berkeley Law had 1,128 students enrolled. Of those, 516 were White, 293 were Asian, 51 were Black and 130 were Hispanic.

In a statement to Fox News, Berkeley Law firmly rejected the allegations, saying its admissions decisions comply with federal law and Proposition 209.

However, the school noted that the laws still allow institutions to build diverse student bodies by considering race-neutral factors, which can include socioeconomic status and personal experiences.

"Our admissions policy is clear that race is not considered in any way in admissions decisions," the school said. "Proposition 209, federal statutes and the Supreme Court’s decisions do not preclude schools from pursuing diversity so long as they give no preferences based on race. Berkeley Law does not do so."

UC Berkeley’s central administration also said the school is "committed to ensuring that every student is admitted based on their merit, and not on their race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin."

"UC Berkeley will spare no effort to provide ample evidence showing that the university complies with all relevant laws, policies and rules governing admissions," the school said.

item.title: ICE arrests Peruvian national accused of illegally voting in 2024 election as DHS cites similar cases
item.description: Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a Peruvian national, was arrested by ICE in Wichita after she allegedly voted illegally in the 2024 Kansas election.
item.content:encoded:
A Peruvian national was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after authorities say she falsely claimed to be a U.S. citizen and illegally voted in the 2024 general election in Kansas, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced Thursday.

Mariana Alexandra Dewey, a lawful permanent resident and citizen of Peru, was arrested by Homeland Security Investigations special agents after authorities determined she unlawfully voted in the Nov. 5, 2024, election in Sedgwick County, according to DHS.

The arrest comes as the Trump administration continues its crackdown on noncitizens accused of illegally voting in U.S. elections.

"This alien violated the sacred right of every American citizen," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a news release.

WATCH: ILLEGAL ALIEN BUSTED IN BATTLEGROUND STATE AFTER ALLEGEDLY COMMITTING VOTER FRAUD

"If even one noncitizen votes, that steals the voice of a U.S. citizen," Mullin continued. "Only American citizens have the right to participate in our political and election processes, and DHS will continue to investigate, seek criminal prosecution and ultimately remove aliens who vote to ensure free, fair and honest elections."

According to DHS, election records showed Dewey submitted a Kansas voter registration application and cast a provisional ballot after certifying, under penalty of perjury, that she was a U.S. citizen.

NONCITIZEN CHARGED WITH VOTING IN MINNESOTA 2024 ELECTION AFTER ADMITTING ‘MISTAKE’ TO INVESTIGATORS

During a subsequent interview with investigators, authorities said Dewey acknowledged she was a lawful permanent resident, not a U.S. citizen, and admitted voting in the 2024 general election. DHS said she later pleaded guilty to disorderly election conduct under Kansas law.

The department said Dewey was taken into ICE custody Sept. 1 after HSI agents located her at a residence in Wichita.

DHS described the arrest as the latest in the administration's effort to crack down on noncitizens accused of illegally voting in American elections.

The department pointed to several recent cases, including enforcement actions involving noncitizens from Colombia, Slovakia, Australia, Mexico and Mauritania, as well as charges against four noncitizens in New Jersey accused of illegally voting in federal elections or falsely claiming U.S. citizenship.

item.title: Trump signs act clearing the way for Medal of Honor monument on National Mall
item.description: Trump signed the act at the National Medal of Honor Museum in Arlington, Texas, after meeting 15 living recipients and touring the facility.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump signed legislation Thursday authorizing the future National Medal of Honor Monument to be located within the Reserve of the National Mall in Washington, D.C., near the Lincoln Memorial, during a ceremony honoring Medal of Honor recipients in Arlington, Texas.

Trump signed the Hershel "Woody" Williams National Medal of Honor Monument Location Act at the National Medal of Honor Museum after touring the museum and meeting more than a dozen recipients.

The legislation does not create the monument itself, which Congress previously authorized in 2021. Instead, it allows the future monument to be located within the Reserve, a protected area of the National Mall that includes some of Washington's most prominent monuments and memorials.

EXCLUSIVE: NEW AMERICA 250 MONUMENT LETS FAMILIES FIND MILITARY RELATIVES IN SECONDS: 'I HAD TEARS IN MY EYES'

Trump greeted and shook hands with recipients before taking the stage for the signing ceremony.

"We're privileged to have with us 15 of the 65 living recipients of the Congressional Medal of Honor," Trump told the audience.

"When I see the recipients of the Congressional Medal, those that are living, many are dead. They died. And they died in battle. Some of the battles are … I read inscriptions of what took place. That level of bravery is incredible," Trump said.

The act is named for Williams, a Marine who received the Medal of Honor for his actions during the Battle of Iwo Jima and was the last surviving World War II Medal of Honor recipient when he died in 2022.

HEGSETH UPGRADES ABBEY GATE MARINES' VALOR AWARDS AFTER 5-YEAR DELAY: 'THOSE DAYS ARE OVER'

Trump recounted Williams' heroism before recognizing members of his family who attended the ceremony.

"In the Battle of Iwo Jima, he carved a path to American victory, literally carved a path so soldiers could get in and win through a deadly gantlet of enemy strongholds," Trump said.

"And back and forth, he went. He just kept going back and forth," Trump continued. "And one machine gun nest after another. He knocked [them] out, and he did it for hours and hours. People said they've never seen anything quite like it."

National Medal of Honor Museum Foundation Chairman Charlotte Jones said 16 of the nation's 65 living Medal of Honor recipients were present at the museum Thursday.

SIX AMERICAN HEROES EVERYONE SHOULD KNOW THIS MEMORIAL DAY, FROM DELTA FORCE TO A WWII BOMBER CREW

"This is not a war museum. This is a museum about heart, about courage, about sacrifice and patriotism," Jones said.

The museum foundation said the effort to create and locate the monument has received eight votes in Congress over six years, all unanimously. The location act itself also passed both chambers without opposition, according to the foundation.

Jones said that bipartisan support reflected the significance of the Medal of Honor and the values associated with it.

"That is the inspirational power of the Medal of Honor," Jones said. "And that is why this project matters."

'BLACK HAWK DOWN' SNIPER SHINES LIGHT ON BRUTAL REALITY OF VIOLENT COMBAT

The future monument will be located near the Lincoln Memorial, though its precise site has not yet been selected. The National Park Service will award the specific site, after which the foundation said it will launch a design competition.

No federal funds will be used to construct the monument, according to the foundation, which will raise the money needed for the project.

Trump also reflected on the sacrifices represented by the recipients gathered for Thursday's ceremony.

9/11 MUSEUM TO OFFER FREE ADMISSION FOR VETERANS AHEAD OF MEMORIAL DAY WEEKEND

"People like this, they stood tall when their country needed heroes," Trump said.

"They carried the wounded out of battle and on their own backs and carried them back and forth," he continued. "They gave their bodies the shields for their brothers at arms. They stood in the way of bullets, purposely standing just like this and taking bullets. And it's amazing. These are amazing."

Trump said the future monument, together with the museum, would provide a permanent way to preserve those stories.

FIRST ON FOX: BEHIND THE SCENES OF ARLINGTON’S MEMORIAL DAY TRIBUTE FOR AMERICA’S 250TH BIRTHDAY

"With this museum and a new monument in Washington, D.C., America will never, ever forget what they did and what they risked and how much they risked, what they meant to their families and what they've meant to our country," Trump said.

The White House told Fox News Digital the signing was intended to recognize the recipients' service and sacrifice.

"Medal of Honor recipients represent the very best of America. President Trump honored their courage today, and a new monument will ensure the nation never forgets their valor and sacrifice," White House spokeswoman Liz Huston said.
